summary: For ages 8-9, picture and bar graphs become SCALED: one square or symbol stands for several units (2, 5 or 10). The core new demand is that a bar's height or a row's length no longer equals the count directly — it must be read THROUGH the scale/key. Learners should read the key first every time, read intermediate values (a half-symbol = half the key; a bar top read by counting the sub-intervals between gridlines), choose a sensible scale (such as 2, 5 or 10) with equally spaced intervals when constructing, and solve one- and two-step comparison, sum and difference problems as explicit 'read each value, then combine' steps. This is the NC Year 3-4 step from single-unit to scaled representations.
misconceptions: Ignores the scale and reads each square/symbol as one unit (or just counts symbols)
Cannot read an intermediate value — rounds a mid-interval bar to a gridline or ignores a part-symbol
Collapses a two-step problem to one step (reads a value but doesn't combine, or does the wrong operation)
Constructs a scaled axis with unequal intervals, so positions no longer map to values

activities.title: Flip the scale: watch the same bars change value
steps: Draw bars for a small data set on squared paper where 'each square = 1'.
Then change the key to 'each square = 5' and re-read every bar: say what each bar now means (e.g. a 4-square bar is now 20, not 4).
State out loud: 'The height on its own doesn't tell me the value — I only know the value once I read it through the scale.'
Optional with an interactive scaled-graph builder: use a scale selector (each square = 2/5/10) that re-labels the axis live, so the same drawn bars instantly re-map to new values.
Choose a sensible scale (e.g. 2, 5 or 10) for a given data set so the largest value fits, mark the axis in equally spaced intervals, and explain why that scale works.
activities.insight: A bar's or symbol's size maps to a value only via the scale; changing the scale re-maps every value, and a sensible scale (e.g. 2, 5 or 10) makes the largest value fit with equal intervals.

activities.title: Reading values between the marks
steps: Read a scaled pictogram with a stated key (e.g. one symbol = 10 children) that includes half-symbols, and give the value of a row ending in a half-symbol: a half-symbol is half the key (with a key of 10 that is 5). Note that with a key of 5 a half-symbol is 2½, which is why pictograms are usually built with an even key so half-symbols land on whole numbers.

Read a scaled bar whose top reaches a specific sub-interval mark between two gridlines — e.g. a bar reaching the 13 mark between the 10 and 15 lines — and state its value by counting the scale's sub-intervals. Separately, note that a bar sitting exactly at the midpoint of 10 and 15 reads as 12½, not a whole number.
Optional with draggable part-symbols or a draggable bar top: hit an exact intermediate value and check it against the key by counting sub-intervals.
activities.insight: Part-symbols and bar tops between gridlines carry real values: a half-symbol is half the key, and you read between gridlines by counting the scale's sub-intervals rather than rounding to the nearest line.

activities.title: Two-step problems as two reads then combine
steps: From a scaled graph, answer a 'how many more' comparison (e.g. how many more chose football than tennis?) by reading each value through the key and finding the difference.
Solve a two-step problem such as 'how many altogether for the top two choices?' by first reading each of the two values separately, then deciding whether to add or subtract, then doing it.
Say the two steps aloud before answering: 'First I read these two values; then I [add/subtract] them.'
Optional with a question panel that shades each bar as it is read before combining, so the two reads are visible as two distinct actions rather than one glance.
activities.insight: The two-step data problems here are two reads followed by one combine (sum or difference); naming both steps helps prevent collapsing it to a single glance or using the wrong operation.

activities.title: Construct a scaled graph from a frequency table
steps: Take a frequency table (e.g. swimming 20, cycling 15) and choose a sensible scale that fits the largest value with equal intervals (e.g. each square = 5, giving 4 squares and 3 squares).
Draw the bars from the baseline with equal width, each reaching the correct scaled position.
Alternatively draw a scaled pictogram with a stated key, using a part-symbol where the value is not a whole multiple of the key.
Check: does each drawn bar/row read back to the original data value when read through the chosen scale?
activities.insight: Constructing a scaled graph requires choosing a workable scale from the data, keeping intervals equal and bars from the baseline, so that positions map back to the intended values.

checkQuestion: First: here is a scaled pictogram of favourite sports where one symbol stands for 5 children (and half-symbols appear) — how many chose football, and how many MORE chose football than tennis? Then: here is the data for two more sports (swimming 20, cycling 15) — draw them as bars on this grid, choosing a sensible scale.
checkAnswer: Interpreting: reads values THROUGH the key (symbols ×5, half-symbol = 2 or 3), and gives the difference for 'how many more'. Translating: draws bars for 20 and 15 using an even scale that fits (e.g. each square = 5), equal width from the baseline.
